object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared or triaged occurrence of something breaking, tracked from origin through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification from the monitoring platform (or a manually raised equivalent) that something may be wrong.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of an alert, generated by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket, potentially linked to an incident as its origin.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier of a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident, from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, one region).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer-urgency classification of an incident, from P1 to P4, based on who's affected, commitments, and SLA breach risk.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident.

object_types.name: Commander
object_types.definition: The named person acting as incident commander for the duration of a declared incident -- a temporary role, not a job title.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service in the catalogue that can be affected by incidents and is owned by a team.

ambiguities.description: Commander's reference mode is assumed to be a 'name', but the transcript only says the commander is 'one person, named' -- it's unclear whether Commander is a full Person/Employee entity with its own employee ID, or just a name string tied to the incident. Clarify whether Commander should be modeled as a full entity type with a proper identifier (e.g., employee ID) rather than just a name.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

ambiguities.description: The conditional mandatory nature of the Commander role (mandatory only for declared/later-state incidents, absent for triage incidents) cannot be fully expressed with a simple mandatory constraint -- it is state-dependent. Clarify whether a subtype (e.g., DeclaredIncident) should be introduced to correctly scope the mandatory commander constraint.

source_references.excerpt: A commander is assigned when it's declared. ... Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised', history 'kept in the timeline as events') but the model only captures the current value on the Incident. Clarify whether a separate Timeline/SeverityHistory entity is needed to track historical changes, or whether current-state-only modeling is acceptable for this exercise.

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: 'Owner' is an overloaded term used both for the Incident Commander (a temporary running role) and the Service Owner (a standing team assignment). While these are modeled as separate fact types (Commander runs Incident vs Service is owned by Team), the transcript flags that this ambiguity causes real confusion operationally -- worth flagging to ensure the two concepts remain clearly distinguished in any generated reports/UI.

source_references.excerpt: Now -- the other 'owner.' ... And in a channel, 'who owns this?' means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: 'Sev' is used colloquially to mean either Severity or Priority, causing miscommunication. This is a terminology/communication issue rather than a modeling gap, but it indicates the two value types (Severity, Priority) must be very clearly labeled and distinguished in any implementation to avoid perpetuating the ambiguity.

source_references.excerpt: Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. ... And people say 'sev' when they mean either.

ambiguities.description: An unresolved business decision: whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is.
